extracted.intended_audience: NPR listeners, fans of comedy, and aspiring stand-up comedians
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and practical considerations for writing and performing stand-up that draws on personal trauma or life events, illustrated by Tig Notaro's Live set and interview. Focuses on vulnerability, audience sensitivity, craft development, and presentation/distribution choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability and personal honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: “I was 'in a very vulnerable, raw place.'” — Notaro framed the set as her own story: “I have cancer — this is my story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using genuine personal experience and emotional honesty can create authority and resonance. The page presents vulnerability as a central strength of the set: rawness can elicit powerful audience responses and authenticity. Example: opening bluntly with diagnosis created a range of reactions and felt truthful rather than performative. Anti-pattern: faking vulnerability or using trauma superficially can ring false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to audience and the risk of offending
rubrics_metrics.description: “I was scared of offending people and confusing people... thinking about people that maybe did have cancer in the audience, or had somebody that they loved that had cancer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When material touches others' trauma, weigh potential harm and confusion. Consider audience composition and whether the piece is framed as your own story (ownership reduces some ethical concerns). Guidance suggests hesitation and reflection are appropriate; the decision to tell should consider both honesty and empathy. Example anti-pattern: obliviously making light of experiences without acknowledging impact on those affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership of the story (performer's prerogative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notaro: 'And then the reality hit me that I have cancer — this is my story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the experience is yours, that ownership permits a different narrative stance; you can assert perspective and authority. The page implies that owning the narrative reduces ethical uncertainty and legitimizes using the material in comedy. Use clear framing to signal this ownership to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolving craft: expanding form and taking your own advice
rubrics_metrics.description: “I started out a dry, deadpan, one-liner comic... And I have allowed myself, by taking my own advice, to write longer jokes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growth and deliberate change in comedic form are signs of craft maturity. Moving from one-liners to longer-form storytelling can allow deeper, personal material to land. Guidance: actively re-evaluate and experiment with structure; taking one's own creative advice can open new possibilities. Anti-pattern: rigidly sticking to an early persona when material demands different forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain core comedic persona/essence while evolving
rubrics_metrics.description: “...I'm gonna do whatever I want to do and hope that the essence of me and what people liked about me in the beginning will come through.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When changing style or content, retain elements of your established comedic persona to preserve audience connection. Balance innovation with continuity so long-time fans still recognize the performer. Scoring note: success judged by whether new material feels like a natural extension, not a total departure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and incorporate audience laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: “I didn't account for laughter... I had been talking to myself... when I got on stage and people laughed, I remember being taken aback. I was like, 'Oh — oh, that's what I was telling you this for, was for the laughter.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and build pauses/phrasing for laughter; test timing in front of real audiences. The interview highlights that performers should factor in the audience's responses as part of structure and pacing. Anti-pattern: writing and delivering material without testing its audience rhythms leads to mis-timed bits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing, silence, and emotional modulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience reaction that night included “nervous laughter, weeping and total silence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skilled use of silence and tonal shifts can create emotional texture and power. The piece demonstrates that juxtaposing humor with silence or tears can amplify impact. Guidance: control pacing deliberately; allow moments for the audience to process. Anti-pattern: constant high-volume joke delivery that doesn't allow emotional beats to land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation, rehearsal, and small-venue testing
rubrics_metrics.description: “I had been talking to myself for so long at my apartment, and I was so focused on getting all of my material down... the second night I did standup... I competed in a standup competition and I got booed off the stage.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearsal and iterative testing are crucial, but success in one context doesn’t guarantee universal acceptance. Use varied venues to refine material and learn what translates. The anecdote shows both the importance of practice and the risks of premature exposure or inappropriate venues (anti-pattern: assuming a single successful performance implies general audience acceptance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer comfort and agency
rubrics_metrics.description: “All I know is that I'm going to do whatever makes me feel comfortable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing material and how to present it should align with the performer’s comfort level and boundaries. This protects authenticity and stamina; comfort can be a metric for whether material is sustainable to perform. Anti-pattern: forcing oneself into territory that feels exploitative or unsafe solely for shock value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding when to disclose sensitive personal information publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: “My first thought when I was diagnosed was, 'Oh, I have to keep this a secret. I don't want to lose work.' ... 'How are we going to keep this a secret?' ... Then that just blew the roof off that.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the professional and personal consequences of public disclosure. The page shows disclosure can rapidly change a performer's career and public awareness; consider timing, potential benefits (visibility, authenticity) and risks (typecasting, privacy loss). This is a strategic/ethical consideration as much as artistic one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and release strategy affect reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Her set was released exclusively on Louis C.K.'s website and later on CD; 'it has just come out on CD.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of distribution platform influences audience size, publicity, and framing. Exclusive releases or endorsement by well-known peers can amplify reach; consider partnerships and formats when planning dissemination. Scoring note: reach and critical attention often depend on platform choices as well as content.

rubrics_metrics.name: External validation and peer/critical recognition as indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Louis C.K.'s tweet: 'In 27 years doing this, I've seen a handful of truly great, masterful standup sets. One was Tig Notaro last night at Largo.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise from respected peers or critics can serve as a signal of quality and can rapidly expand visibility. However, such validation is supplementary and not the sole measure of success; balance peer praise with audience connection and personal satisfaction.
